comments.text_zh: 大家好！前几天我和一个朋友聊天 [1]，他分享了这个想法，我觉得它来自一个 Veritasium 视频 [2]：如果你随机取 1000 个人，按他们的总体成功程度排名，排在最前面的几乎总是那些极其幸运的人（也就是说：你能登顶靠的是运气，而不只是努力）。虽然背后的数学极其简单（就是一个加权求和），代码 [3] 也一样简单，但我认为“光靠努力并不能保证成功”这个想法很有力量。另外，我觉得这个小应用玩起来挺有意思。希望这个思想实验能帮助大家反思生活中随机性这回事，也许还能帮你和朋友们聊出一些有趣的对话！很期待听到你们的反馈。[1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO] [3] [LINK]
comments.text: Hi guys! I was talking with a friend the other day [1] and he shared this idea, I think it comes from a Veritasium video [2], that if you took 1.000 random people and ranked them by their overall success, the top ones would almost always be extremely lucky (i.e.: you get to the top by being lucky, not by hard work alone) Although the math behind it is extremely simple (just a weighted sum), as well as the code [3], I think the idea that hard work alone doesn't guarantee success is a powerful one. Plus, I think the app is fun to play with. Hope this thought experiment helps reflect about the whole idea of randomness in life, and maybe help spark a few interesting conversations with friends! It'd be great to hear your feedback. [1] [LINK] [2] [VIDEO] [3] [LINK]

comments.quote_zh: 如果你只把结果的 5% 归因于运气，那么那些结果最好的人就是最幸运的人之一
comments.text_zh: 我看过一个视频，里面解释说，如果你只把结果的 5% 归因于运气，那么那些结果最好的人就是最幸运的人之一。很难界定运气在任一具体情境中到底有多重要，但如果你把我们生活的方方面面都视为运气的一部分——我认为这正是人们在争论运气与努力时所指的意思——那我觉得实际上远高于 5%。也就是说，出生地点/时间、父母、家庭、出生时的社会经济地位、学校、朋友、老师、健康、事情的时机、偶然相遇——这些大多都超出你的控制。Hacker News 上可能有人会想，自己多年来努力学软件工程、花时间建立人脉、练习面试题、申请了好几个地方、面试表现很好，然后拿到了一份高薪工作。这些都算努力的一部分，而且往往是成功的必要部分。这感觉不像是你靠运气得到了什么。但幸运的部分主要是前面我提到的那些东西——出生时发生的事，或者因为别人的行为而发生的事。比如，如果你出生时就是富裕的美国白人，那你的运气值从一开始就很高。然后也许在某个时刻，你遇到了一位以有意义的方式帮助你的老师，或者你认识了一个影响你决策的朋友。别忘了，还有同样合格、同样努力学习、练习、做同样事情的人
comments.text: I saw a video explaining where if you attribute just 5% of outcomes to luck, then the people who have the best outcomes are among the luckiest people. It's hard to define just how much luck would matter in any given situation, but if you consider every aspect of our lives as part of luck, which I think is what people mean when they debate luck vs hard work, then I think it's a lot higher than 5% actually. That is, things like place/time of birth, parents, family, socioeconomic status at birth, schools, friends, teachers, health, timing of things, chance encounters - these things are all mostly outside of your control. Someone on hacker news might be thinking how they worked hard for years to learn software engineering, spent time networking, practiced interview questions, applied to several places, performed well in the interviews, and landed a lucrative job. And that's all part of hard work and it's often a necessary part of success. It doesn't feel like you lucked into anything. But the lucky part was mostly all the stuff I mentioned before - things that happened at birth, or things that happened because of others' actions. If you're born an affluent white American, for example, your luck meter is highly filled from the start. Then maybe at some point you had a teacher that helped you in a meaningful way, or you met a friend that influenced your decision making. And let's not forget there are people who are just as qualified, who study hard, practice, do all the same things

comments.text_zh: 据我所知，这个趋势有充分支持[1]。这个趋势是否在你内心表现为一种失败主义态度，是个人的选择。但与此同时，无论你持什么态度，都不会神奇地消除你与生俱来的那些劣势，所以仅仅把它斥为失败主义态度是适得其反的。危险在于忽视这些文章中的自我中心偏差倾向[2]。成功人士会假定是他们的价值观和伦理让他们走向成功，但事实可能并非如此。不过这就引出了一个问题：我们该听谁关于成功的建议？富人？科学研究[3]？我之前在 Hacker News 上读过一个帖子（碰巧是关于 Paul Graham，另一位 ycombinator 创始人），它也许比我更能表达这些想法[4] [1]: [LINK] [2]: [VIDEO] [3]: [LINK] [4]: [LINK]
comments.text: It's a trend that's well supported afaik [1]. Whether or not that trend manifests inside you as a defeatist attitude is a personal choice. But at the same time, whatever attitude you have isn't going to magically get rid of whatever disadvantages you were born into, so simply dismissing it a defeatist attitude is counterproductive. The danger is ignoring the tendency of egocentric bias in these articles[2]. Successful people assume that their values and ethics are what led them to success, when that may not be true. Though that then bears the question: who do we listen to for advice on success? Rich people? Scientific studies [3]? A thread I read on a previous hackernews post (coincidentally about Paul Graham, another founder of ycombinator) perhaps puts these ideas in better words than I [4] [1]: [LINK] [2]: [VIDEO] [3]: [LINK] [4]: [LINK]
